Boosted uniform line charge (λ=γλ0​,I=λu)

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Relativistic electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
An infinite uniform line with proper charge per unit length λ0​ moving axially at speed u has Lorentz-contracted density λ=γλ0​ and current I=λu. Transverse distance r is unchanged by the boost. The rest electric field λ0​r/(2πϵ0​r) transforms into E=λr/(2πϵ0​r) and B=u×E/c2. This equals the magnetic field μ0​Iφ​/(2πr) from Ampère's law. The formulas concern a uniform stationary current pattern, not an accelerating finite filament's radiation.

Neutral current filament in a boosted frame (λ′=−γuI/c2,I′=γI)

Words: 76
Boosted uniform line charge OurBigBook.com
For an ideal infinite filament with zero line charge density and current I in a laboratory frame, the line-integrated four-current is (0,I) in temporal/axial components. An axial boost of speed u gives the title density and current. The laboratory magnetic field μ0​Iφ​/(2πr) therefore becomes both an electric field from λ′ and a magnetic field from I′. Charge neutrality is frame-dependent for a current-carrying system. A model built from oppositely charged moving and resting populations makes this result explicit; the charge of each fixed material particle set remains invariant.

Polarization-magnetization tensor (Mμν)

Words: 64
Relativistic electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
An antisymmetric tensor combines the electric polarization and magnetization of a medium. For Minkowski metric (−,+,+,+) and units with light speed one, choose Mi0=Pi​ and Mij=ϵijk​Mk​, together with Fi0​=Ei​ and Fij​=ϵijk​Bk​. Then the Lorentz scalar interaction is MμνFμν​/2=P⋅E+M⋅B. The bound charge and bound current have four-current jbμ​=∂ν​Mμν, giving ρb​=−∇⋅P and Jb​=∂t​P+∇×M. This current is identically conserved because partial derivatives commute and M is antisymmetric.

Electromagnetic minimal coupling

Words: 61
Relativistic charged-particle action OurBigBook.com
Electromagnetic minimal coupling replaces the free kinetic momentum in an action or Hamiltonian by a combination involving the electromagnetic potential. For L=−mx˙ax˙a​​−qAa​x˙a, the canonical covector is Pa​=−mx˙a​/x˙2​−qAa​, so Pa​+qAa​ recovers the potential-independent covector. Under Aa​↦Aa​+∂a​χ, the action changes by an endpoint term. The fixed-endpoint equations are the relativistic Lorentz force equation and are gauge invariant.

Retarded potentials of a point electric dipole (t0​=t−r/c)

Words: 90
Retarded potential OurBigBook.com
An ideal electric dipole at the origin with smooth electric dipole moment p(t) has Lorenz gauge electric potential and magnetic vector potential, for r>0,
ϕ=4πϵ0​1​(r2n⋅p(t0​)​+crn⋅p′(t0​)​),A=4πrμ0​​p′(t0​),n=rr​.
(5)
For a short proof, place electric charges sq at sp/(2q), s=±1, and let q→∞ with p fixed. The corresponding retarded times are t0​+sn⋅p(t0​)/(2qc)+O(q−2). Each Liénard–Wiechert potential has denominator r−s(n⋅p+rn⋅p′/c)/(2q)+O(q−2). The opposite q/r terms cancel, leaving the displayed electric potential. The products of signed electric charge and velocity add, giving the displayed magnetic vector potential. Bounded time derivatives on the relevant interval justify the Taylor expansions.

Arrival-time compression for a moving source (dta​/dt=1−n⋅β)
Words: 83
Retarded time OurBigBook.com
For a stationary distant detector, the arrival time of a light signal emitted at (t,x(t)) is ta​=t+∣xD​−x(t)∣/c. Its derivative is dta​/dt=1−n⋅u/c, where n points from the source to the detector. This exact relation follows by differentiating the distance; a constant viewing direction is a far-field approximation. For a source approaching near the speed of light, a long emission interval can correspond to a short arrival interval. Combining it with the 1/γ cone of relativistic beaming yields synchrotron pulse compression of order r/(cγ3).

Electric field of a uniformly moving point charge
Words: 77
Liénard-Wiechert field OurBigBook.com
Let R join the instantaneous position of charge q to the field point, with constant β=v/c. Transforming its rest-frame Coulomb field gives
E=4πϵ0​[R2−∣β×R∣2]3/2q(1−β2)R​,B=v×E/c2.
(9)
The electric field is radial from the current position, reduced along the velocity and enhanced transversely. This present-position form is compatible with the causal retarded solution specifically because motion is uniform. There is no acceleration-dependent radiation field, although the moving charge has a magnetic field and transports electromagnetic energy.

Lorenz-gauge potentials for a circularly polarized plane wave (Φ=0,A=ω−2∂t​E)

Words: 63
Lorenz gauge condition OurBigBook.com
For a transverse monochromatic electromagnetic wave with angular frequency ω=0, ∂t2​E=−ω2E. The displayed electric potential and magnetic vector potential therefore give −∇Φ−∂t​A=E. Transversality gives ∇⋅A=0, so the Lorenz gauge holds. For E=E0​(cosθ,sinθ,0) and θ=ωt−Kz, taking a curl yields B=(K/ω)z×E. The vacuum Maxwell equations require K2=ω2/c2. The field has circular polarization, with ∣B∣=∣E∣/c and perpendicular electric and magnetic directions.

Curved-spacetime electromagnetic potential wave equation (□Aν​−Rαν​Aα​=−μ0​Jν​)

Lorenz gauge condition OurBigBook.com
With convention ∇μFμν​=−μ0​Jν​, write the electromagnetic field tensor as Fμν​=∇μ​Aν​−∇ν​Aμ​. Commuting the contracted covariant derivatives gives ∇μ∇ν​Aμ​=∇ν​(∇μAμ​)+Rαν​Aα​. The Lorenz gauge condition removes the gradient-of-divergence term, leaving the displayed wave equation for a covector field. A locally inertial coordinate system does not eliminate the Ricci tensor term.

Index conventions for the electromagnetic field tensor

Words: 64
Electromagnetic field tensor OurBigBook.com
Choose coordinates xμ=(ct,x) and Minkowski metric η=diag(1,−1,−1,−1). With the convention F0i=−Ei​/c and Fij=−ϵijk​Bk​, lowering both tensor indices gives F0i​=+Ei​/c while leaving Fij​=Fij. An array with all upper indices cannot be used unchanged as the corresponding array with all lower indices. The propagation Lorentz four-vector nμ=(1,s) for unit spatial direction s similarly has nμ​=(1,−s). These signs matter in contractions that encode Maxwell equations.

First-order Maxwell action (S=16π1​∫−g​[FabFab​−2Fab(∇a​Ab​−∇b​Aa​)])
Words: 58
Maxwell action OurBigBook.com
Vary the antisymmetric auxiliary electromagnetic field tensor and the electromagnetic four-potential independently. The first variation sets Fab​=∇a​Ab​−∇b​Aa​ algebraically, and variation of the potential gives ∇b​Fab=0. Substitution of the algebraic equation reduces the first-order action to the usual negative quadratic Maxwell action. Lorentz force (F=q(E+v×B))

Words: 8k Articles: 78
Electromagnetic field tensor OurBigBook.com
The Lorentz force is the force exerted by an electric field E and a magnetic field B on a body with electric charge q and velocity v. In SI units its form in nonrelativistic classical mechanics, using mass m and Newton's second law, is
F=q(E+v×B),mdtdv​=q(E+v×B).
(14)
Both fields are evaluated at the body's position at the current time. The electric field contributes qE even at rest, whereas the magnetic force depends on velocity through a cross product. [ref]; [ref].
For a concrete charged particle in a uniform magnetic field, use nondimensionalization to stipulate m=q=B=1, magnetic field B=(0,0,1), zero electric field, initial position (0,0,0), and initial velocity (1,0,0). These are rescaled quantities, not an assertion that the mass, electric charge, and magnetic field have the same physical units. At the start, (1,0,0)×(0,0,1)=(0,−1,0), so the magnetic acceleration points toward −y. The resulting circular motion is
r(t)=(sint,cost−1,0),v(t)=(cost,−sint,0),a(t)=(−sint,−cost,0).
(15)
At t=π/2 the position is (1,−1,0) and the velocity is (0,−1,0); at t=π the position is (0,−2,0) and the velocity is (−1,0,0). Thus the circle has center (0,−1,0) and radius one. Viewed from +z toward the xy plane, the motion is clockwise. Changing only the electric charge to q=−1 gives position (sint,1−cost,0) and reverses the bending to counterclockwise.
Adding initial velocity vz​=0.5 leaves the transverse circular motion unchanged and gives
r(t)=(sint,cost−1,0.5t),v(t)=(cost,−sint,0.5).
(16)
This is a helix of transverse radius one, cyclotron frequency ωc​=1, and transverse period T=2π; the advance along z in one turn is π. The parallel component of velocity stays constant because the magnetic force has no parallel component: there is no magnetic acceleration along the magnetic field. If the initial velocity were entirely parallel to the magnetic field, the magnetic force would vanish and the path would be straight. [ref].
More generally, with zero electric field, no other forces, and a uniform constant magnetic field of magnitude B>0, decompose velocity into perpendicular and parallel components. For nonzero electric charge q, the perpendicular speed v⊥​ determines the gyroradius, while the cyclotron frequency is an angular frequency:
r=∣q∣Bmv⊥​​,ωc​=m∣q∣B​,T=ωc​2π​=∣q∣B2πm​.
(17)
These are nonrelativistic formulas; see the relativistic cyclotron orbit for the correction. The beauty is that increasing perpendicular speed increases the radius in exactly the proportion needed to leave the period unchanged. Conversely, known magnetic field, perpendicular speed, and measured radius determine the magnitude of the electric charge divided by mass. This makes the same geometry useful for comparing bodies with different electric charge and mass.
Two short checks explain the result. First, the cross product gives v×B=(−sint,−cost,0) for both stipulated positive-electric charge paths, exactly their acceleration. Second, the transverse magnetic force supplies the centripetal acceleration, so mv⊥2​/r=∣q∣v⊥​B; for v⊥​>0 this gives the gyroradius, and ωc​=v⊥​/r gives the cyclotron frequency.
Magnetic forces do no work: the instantaneous power of the magnetic part of the Lorentz force vanishes because a cross product is perpendicular to its first argument. The work-energy theorem therefore gives
dtdK​=F⋅v=qE⋅v+qv⋅(v×B)=qE⋅v,K=21​m∣v∣2.
(18)
The dot product v⋅(v×B) is zero at every instant, rather than only after a full turn. With zero electric field and no other forces, the kinetic energy and speed remain constant; the electric field can increase or decrease kinetic energy according to the sign of qE⋅v. In the two stipulated examples the constant kinetic energy is respectively K=1/2 and K=5/8 in rescaled units. The extra parallel velocity raises kinetic energy without changing the gyroradius or the cyclotron frequency.
For an electric example in rescaled units, stipulate m=q=1, zero magnetic field, constant electric field E=(2,0,0), no other forces, and rest at t=0. The Lorentz force gives acceleration (2,0,0) and velocity (2t,0,0), hence kinetic energy K=2t2 and power dK/dt=4t=qE⋅v. At t=1, the kinetic energy has risen from zero to two: the electric field has done positive work.
The existing electromagnetic field tensor formulation expresses the same interaction covariantly. For four-momentum pμ and four-velocity uμ, using proper time τ, the Lorentz force law is
dτdpμ​=qFμνuν​.
(19)
Its spatial and temporal components are
dtdp​=q(E+v×B),dtdE​=qE⋅v.
(20)
Magnetic-slab transmission threshold (mv/(∣q∣B)>b)
Words: 75
Lorentz force OurBigBook.com
A nonrelativistic charged particle entering a uniform magnetic region normally at one plane follows a circle of radius r=mv/(∣q∣B). If the field extends through a normal thickness b, the particle enters the strict region beyond the far plane only for r>b. Equality gives tangency, not crossing. For transmission, its deflection angle obeys sinθ=b/r. The result assumes a sharp field boundary, fixed speed in the magnetic region and no electric field there.

Anderson positron track experiment
Words: 866 Articles: 2
Magnetic rigidity OurBigBook.com
The Anderson positron track experiment identified a light positively charged particle, now called the Positron, by combining magnetic bending, loss of kinetic energy in lead, and particle range. Each observation answered a different question: bending constrained momentum, the lead supplied a direction of travel, and particle range tested the proposed mass.
Carl David Anderson's The Positive Electron (1933), pp. 491–493, describes the 1932 discovery in a vertical cloud chamber with a 15,000gauss magnetic field. A 6mm lead plate separated two photographed track segments. The effective viewing depth was 1cm along the magnetic field, with 14cm transverse diameter: this restricted out-of-plane motion. The photographic readout supplied curvature on both sides. Comparisons with electron tracks under the same conditions constrained ionization; specific ionization was not directly measured for these events. He tested accidental alignment of unrelated tracks and rejected a reversed electron interpretation requiring an increase of kinetic energy in lead. Assuming unit electric charge, the mass bound was about twenty electron masses, rather than an exact mass determination. The paper credits Robert Andrews Millikan with the design and Seth Henry Neddermeyer with assistance.[ref]
Preparation used rapid piston expansion and a water–alcohol mixture in the cloud chamber; cooling permitted droplets to form along ionization trails. A camera photographed these droplets. Initially, expansions occurred at random, so many photographs contained no tracks. Later counter triggering improved the useful yield.[ref]
In The Production and Properties of Positrons, his 1936 lecture, Carl David Anderson describes the chamber inside an electromagnet and explains why the lead plate was decisive: after losing kinetic energy, a particle bent more sharply. He describes a proton hypothesis predicting only 5mm of particle range, against an observed path longer than 50mm. These are historical values from the lecture, not the stipulated example below. The point was the incompatibility of particle range with the momentum inferred from curvature, rather than positive electric charge alone.[ref]

Gravity does not justify assuming that every cosmic ray track travels downward.
The lead plate adds a physical ordering. For a single particle crossing a passive absorber without an accelerating interaction, the outgoing momentum is smaller, so the outgoing gyroradius is smaller in the same magnetic field. The less curved segment comes first. Once this direction is assigned, the cross product in the Lorentz force determines the sign of electric charge. For the convention below, B=Bz points out of the page; at upward velocity v=vy​, v×B=vBx. Bending to the right therefore means positive electric charge.
Magnetic forces do no work: the change of kinetic energy occurs through interaction with the material, not through the bending magnetic field. The ideal construction suppresses multiple scattering, kinetic energy fluctuations, and loss of kinetic energy in the gas. In an actual analysis one compares arcs away from the plate and allows a change of tangent from multiple scattering; one cannot interpret every kink as a change of electric charge. Short visible arcs, uncertain projection and small bending also limit a determination of magnetic rigidity.

A velocity selector uses perpendicular electric field and magnetic field to transmit a narrow range of speeds along a chosen beam direction. Assume uniform static electric field E=Ey​ and magnetic field Bs​=Bs​z, with E,Bs​>0, and an incident velocity v=vx. The cross product gives v×Bs​=−vBs​y​, so the transverse Lorentz force is
Fy​=q(E−vBs​),Fy​=0 ⟹ v0​=Bs​E​.
(23)
For an electron, the electric force points downward and the magnetic force upward. A faster electron initially bends upward; a slower one initially bends downward. At the selected speed, both forces cancel along the whole straight trajectory. The cancellation is independent of mass and nonzero electric charge; it selects velocity, not a particular charge-to-mass ratio. A component of velocity parallel to the magnetic field is not constrained by the cancellation, so the incident beam must also have its direction restricted.
A real exit slit accepts a finite range of speeds and incident directions. A zero displacement at one screen alone does not establish zero force throughout the path: a curved trajectory could return to that screen position. The ideal velocity selector interpretation requires a straight aligned beam, known overlapping electric field and magnetic field, and sufficiently narrow entrance and exit slits. Its useful role in the Thomson charge-to-mass experiment teaching model is to supply speed independently of the subsequent magnetic bending.

Lorentz force OurBigBook.com
The Thomson charge-to-mass experiment infers the magnitude of an electron's charge-to-mass ratio by combining electric and magnetic deflection of cathode rays. The central idea is to determine speed separately from magnetic curvature: a known speed turns the observed gyroradius into a measurement of e/m.
In 1897, J. J. Thomson used two grounded slits in an evacuated glass tube, then aluminium plates 5cm long, 2cm wide and 1.5cm apart. A battery supplied their electric potential difference. Deflected cathode rays produced a phosphorescence patch on the glass; an external scale and movable luminous pointer recorded its position in darkness. Greater evacuation reduced gas electrical conductivity that screened the electric field; reversing plate polarity reversed deflection. External coils supplied the magnetic field, calibrated by induction against larger coils. He adjusted equal electric and magnetic deflections. [ref]
His comparison included air, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and aluminium versus platinum cathodes, supporting a common carrier. He explicitly noted uncorrected magnetic bending outside the plates. His tables give m/e, the reciprocal of the magnitude used here. The inferred ratio alone could not separate electric charge from mass. [ref]
To connect this readout with the Lorentz force, derive a simple nonrelativistic model in modern SI notation. Let the uniform deflecting region have length ℓ, followed by a field-free drift of length L. Assume a narrow speed distribution, small deflection angles, negligible collisions, and matching electric and magnetic field profiles. For an electron with speed v, the electric acceleration has magnitude eE/m, the transit time is approximately ℓ/v, and the subsequent drift adds exit transverse velocity times L/v. Thus the displacement magnitudes measured separately with only electric field or only magnetic field are
∣yE​∣=mv2eE​ℓ(L+2ℓ​),∣yB​∣≃mveB​ℓ(L+2ℓ​).
(24)
The electric expression follows from constant transverse acceleration; the magnetic expression uses its small-deflection approximation. Equal displacement magnitudes then give
v≃BE​,me​≃B2ℓ(L+ℓ/2)E∣yE​∣​.
(25)
This is an ideal derivation of the comparison principle, not a numerical reanalysis of the historical tube. Different exterior magnetic field profiles invalidate cancellation of the common geometrical factor. The comparison determines e/m through deflection and the known apparatus dimensions; it does not require a downstream semicircle.
For a second, deliberately different teaching geometry, combine a velocity selector with a separate region containing only a uniform magnetic field Ba​ perpendicular to the selected velocity. Here Bs​ belongs to the velocity selector, while Ba​ belongs to the analyzer: they need not be equal. The magnetic Lorentz force supplies the centripetal acceleration, so
rmv2​=evBa​,me​=Ba​rv​=Bs​Ba​rE​.
(26)
If the analyzer turns the beam through a semicircle before it hits a screen in the entry plane, the separation D between entrance and impact is the diameter: r=D/2. For a shorter observed arc, the screen displacement is not generally a radius; fit the appropriate circle geometry. This two-stage velocity selector and curvature apparatus is an original ideal teaching model, not a claim that Thomson's Fig. 2 used a separate selector and semicircular analyzer.
For a worked example, stipulate E=2.00×103Vm−1, Bs​=1.00×10−3T, Ba​=2.00×10−4T, and D=0.1136m. The selected speed and inferred charge-to-mass ratio magnitude are
v=1.00×10−32.00×103​=2.00×106ms−1,r=0.0568m,

me​=(2.00×10−4)(0.0568)2.00×106​≃1.76×1011Ckg−1.

The bending direction gives the sign of the electric charge once the magnetic field direction is known. Scaling both e and m by the same positive factor preserves every displayed trajectory, so an independent electric charge measurement is required to determine mass separately.
The curvature formula assumes nonrelativistic momentum p=mv. At higher speeds, the relativistic cyclotron orbit gives p=γmv=eBa​r, hence e/m=γv/(Ba​r), where γ is the Lorentz factor; the ideal straight-through selection v=E/Bs​ still follows from vanishing Lorentz force. The stipulated speed is about 0.0067 times the speed of light, making γ−1 about 2.2×10−5. For this example the nonrelativistic approximation is adequate, but no massive particle can be selected at E/Bs​≥c. Finite slit widths, collisions with residual gas, uncertain magnetic field calibration, and fields outside the ideal boundaries limit a real inference; repeat at several selected speeds and analyzer strengths to test consistency of e/m rather than trusting one spot position.
Lenard cathode-ray window experiment
Words: 1k Articles: 1
Lorentz force OurBigBook.com
The Lenard cathode-ray window experiment lets cathode rays leave a gas-discharge tube through a thin aluminium foil while preserving the tube's vacuum. This separates production from propagation.
Philipp Lenard's lecture, delivered on 28 May 1906, describes sealing a small hole in a metal plate with aluminium foil. Luminous phosphor grains first rested on the window, then glowed above it in air. His improved tube separated production and observation chambers; coated paper served as a fluorescent screen. An aperture revealed spreading beyond a narrow straight beam. Evacuating the observation chamber reduced spreading and attenuation without interrupting production. Interposed layers and stepped foil stacks gave shadow comparisons; approximate scaling with mass had exceptions.[ref]
The experimental advantage is unusually clean: reducing the gas content in the observation chamber tests whether gas is needed to carry the cathode rays, while retaining the conditions needed to generate them. The window is a boundary that transmits some electrons while confining the source environment. A spot outside establishes a transmitted effect; the aperture and changed observation environment provide additional ways to distinguish propagation from the source's behavior. This logic is useful whenever a complicated source would otherwise be changed by the very intervention intended to test the emitted beam.
Several inferences require care. A darker fluorescent screen can mean fewer arriving electrons, less deposited energy per electron, or redistribution by electron scattering beyond the observed area. A visible endpoint depends on the screen's sensitivity and background. It is not an intrinsic electron range independent of initial kinetic energy, gas density, and observation geometry. For a modern comparison, measure a reference at fixed source conditions, use background subtraction, and compare the whole luminous patch as well as a small central region. A wider collection area tests redistribution; changing source-to-screen separation also changes collection geometry. These are proposed controls for interpreting a readout, not additional historical observations attributed to Lenard.
Nor is fluorescence a unique signature of cathode rays: X-rays can also excite it. Lenard notes that a later tube could transmit both, and that slow cathode rays failed to pass its window.[ref] In modern terms, cathode rays are electrons carrying negative electric charge, whereas X-rays are photons with zero electric charge. Magnetic bending of the incident electrons, interpreted through the Lorentz force, supplies a discrimination that brightness alone cannot. Passage through foil alone determines neither the sign of electric charge nor its magnitude, and it does not measure charge-to-mass ratio. The separate Thomson charge-to-mass experiment explains that inference. Even a measured charge-to-mass ratio needs an independent electric charge measurement to determine mass.

They cut Hall bars and made indium contacts. Low-field measurements established number density and charge carrier mobility. A perpendicular magnetic field sweep measured transverse and longitudinal sheet resistivities at several temperatures. The longitudinal minimum remained finite at the lowest temperature: zero-temperature vanishing was unresolved. This established anomalous transport, without directly measuring excitation electric charge.[ref]

Stress conservation implies the source-free Maxwell equations if the matrix Fac​ is invertible; otherwise it only forces the field divergence into that matrix's kernel. Conversely source-free Maxwell equations always imply stress conservation.
Gauge-compensated time translation in electromagnetism (δAν​=αF0ν​)

Electromagnetic stress-energy tensor OurBigBook.com
With signature (+,−,−,−) and L=−Fμν​Fμν/4, combine a time translation α∂0​Aν​ with the gauge transformation of parameter −αA0​. Its Noether current is Jμ=−FμνF0ν​−δ0μ​L, the gauge-invariant energy current. The density is (∣E∣2+∣B∣2)/2. On the source-free field equations it differs from the canonical translation current by ∂ν​(A0​Fμν), an antisymmetric superpotential divergence, so total energies agree when the boundary term vanishes.

Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic fields

Words: 234 Articles: 4
Relativistic electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
Lorentz boosts mix transverse electric and magnetic field components.

Longitudinal solenoid field under an axial boost

Words: 60
Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic fields OurBigBook.com
An ideal long solenoid has B=μ0​nI, with axial turn density n. Under an axial boost, turn density becomes n′=γn. The transverse circulation path is unchanged while a turn's charge-circulation rate, measured relative to its moving material, becomes I′=I/γ. Thus n′I′=nI and the axial magnetic field remains unchanged. Equivalently, the ideal transverse current-sheet density is invariant under this boost. End effects are excluded.

Longitudinal capacitor field under a normal boost

Words: 61
Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic fields OurBigBook.com
For ideal oppositely charged parallel plates, the normal electric field is σ/ϵ0​. A boost along that normal leaves each transverse plate area unchanged. Invariance of total charge therefore preserves surface charge density and the normal electric field. The plate separation contracts, but the large-plate field does not depend on that separation. Including longitudinal contraction in a voltage argument while holding voltage fixed would impose an unsupported extra assumption.

Relativistic charge density of counterstreaming beams (λ′=−γvI/c2)

Words: 64
Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic fields OurBigBook.com
Two equal opposite line charge densities moving in opposite directions have zero net line charge but a nonzero total current I. Under a longitudinal Lorentz boost, the charge-current four-vector gives λ′=γ(λ−vI/c2)=−γvI/c2. Equivalently, for lab densities n and speeds ±u, their separate boosted number densities are γn(1∓vu/c2). Their imbalance creates the boosted radial electric field, consistently with Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic fields and Gauss's law.

[Bn′​]=0,[Et′​]=v×[Bt′​].
